title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids
html:
How to use this sheet: you do not need any background to read it. Start with Key Terms. Each concept then goes: plain English → analogy → 3 core points → for every formula: what it says, when to use it, what each letter means, an everyday example, a step-by-step MCAT example and the trap → where to practice. Read top to bottom once, then use the formulas as a reference.

Key terms (read first)

TermPlain meaning
MoleculeA group of atoms stuck together by chemical bonds.
ProteinA long chain of amino acids folded into a specific 3D shape. The shape decides the job (carrying oxygen, speeding reactions, building muscle).
Amino acidOne link in the protein chain. Every amino acid has the same core (a central carbon called the α-carbon, holding an amino group –NH₂, a carboxyl group –COOH and a hydrogen) plus one variable part, the side chain.
Side chain (R group)The part that differs between the 20 amino acids. It decides whether the amino acid is oily, water-loving, acidic or basic.
Polar / nonpolarPolar = has uneven charge, mixes with water. Nonpolar = oily, avoids water.
Chiral / stereocenterA carbon bonded to four different groups. Like your left and right hands, it has a mirror image that cannot be stacked on top of it.
L / D and R / STwo different naming systems for the "handedness" of a chiral carbon. L/D compares the molecule to a reference sugar; R/S ranks the four attached groups. They do not always match.
H⁺ (proton)A hydrogen atom that has lost its electron. Acids give away H⁺; bases pick it up.
pHA number for how much H⁺ is in a solution. Low pH (0–6) = acidic, lots of H⁺. 7 = neutral. High pH (8–14) = basic, little H⁺. Blood is 7.4.
pKaThe pH at which a group is exactly half "holding its H⁺" and half "has let go". Low pKa = lets go of H⁺ easily.
Protonated / deprotonatedHolding its H⁺ / has given its H⁺ away.
ZwitterionA molecule with both a + and a − charge at the same time (net charge 0).
Isoelectric point (pI)The pH at which a molecule's charges cancel out exactly (net charge 0).
Peptide bondThe link between two amino acids (a C(=O)–NH amide bond). Making it releases one water molecule.
Hydrogen bond (H-bond)A weak attraction between an H on N or O and a nearby N or O. Weak alone, strong in large numbers, like Velcro.
Energy / free energy (G)The "usable" energy in a system. Processes run on their own when free energy goes down.
EnzymeA protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
Substrate (S)The molecule an enzyme works on.
Product (P)What the substrate becomes after the reaction.
Active siteThe pocket on the enzyme where the substrate sits and reacts.
Activation energy (Ea)The energy "hill" a reaction must climb before it can happen.
Inhibitor (I)A molecule that slows an enzyme down.
Concentration [X]How much of X is dissolved per liter. Square brackets mean "concentration of". Units: M (moles per liter), mM (thousandths of M), μM (millionths of M).
LigandAny molecule that binds to a protein (O₂ is hemoglobin's ligand).

The 20 amino acids: full names and abbreviations

Each amino acid has a full name, a 3-letter code and a 1-letter code. The sheet uses the 1-letter codes in lists, so look them up here.

Full name3-letter code1-letter codeSide-chain familyWhat to remember
GlycineGlyGNonpolarSide chain is just H; the only achiral one; flexible, common in turns
AlanineAlaANonpolarSmall methyl (–CH₃) side chain
ValineValVNonpolarBranched; oily
LeucineLeuLNonpolarBranched; oily
IsoleucineIleINonpolarBranched; has a second chiral carbon
MethionineMetMNonpolarContains sulfur; the start amino acid of almost every protein (codon AUG)
ProlineProPNonpolarSide chain loops back to the backbone N, making a rigid ring; breaks α-helices
PhenylalaninePheFNonpolarBenzene ring (aromatic)
TryptophanTrpWNonpolarLargest; double ring (aromatic); absorbs UV light at 280 nm
SerineSerSPolar, uncharged–OH group; common phosphorylation site
ThreonineThrTPolar, uncharged–OH group; second chiral carbon; phosphorylation site
CysteineCysCPolar, uncharged–SH group; two cysteines form a disulfide (S–S) bond; the only L-amino acid that is R
AsparagineAsnNPolar, unchargedAmide version of aspartate
GlutamineGlnQPolar, unchargedAmide version of glutamate
TyrosineTyrYPolar, unchargedAromatic ring with –OH; phosphorylation site
Aspartate (aspartic acid)AspDAcidic (−1 at pH 7.4)Side-chain –COOH, pKa ≈ 3.7–3.9 (tables differ slightly)
Glutamate (glutamic acid)GluEAcidic (−1 at pH 7.4)Side-chain –COOH, pKa ≈ 4.1–4.3 (tables differ slightly)
LysineLysKBasic (+1 at pH 7.4)Side-chain –NH₃⁺, pKa ≈ 10.5
ArginineArgRBasic (+1 at pH 7.4)Guanidinium group, pKa ≈ 12.5; the most basic
HistidineHisHBasic (mostly neutral at pH 7.4)Imidazole ring, pKa ≈ 6.0; often in enzyme active sites because it can take or give H⁺ near body pH

A) CORE CONCEPTS

Concept 1: What an amino acid looks like, and its "handedness"

In plain English: Every amino acid is built the same way except for one swappable piece, the side chain. Most amino acids also come in a left-handed and a right-handed version, and your body only uses one of them.

Analogy: Amino acids are LEGO bricks. Every brick has the same connectors (the backbone that links into a chain) but a different decoration on top (the side chain). The decoration decides what the brick does in the final model.

Official definition: The 20 standard amino acids share an α-carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, an H and a variable R group. All except glycine are chiral, and ribosomes (the cell's protein-building machines) use only the L-form.

Core idea (3 points):

  • All are L. Every amino acid in your proteins is the L-form. In the R/S system almost all are S. The one exception is cysteine, which is R, because its side chain contains sulfur, and sulfur outranks the oxygens of the carboxyl group in the R/S ranking rules (called CIP rules, which rank atoms by atomic number).
  • Glycine is the odd one out. Its side chain is just H, so its α-carbon holds two identical H atoms. Without four different groups it has no handedness (achiral).
  • Four families by side chain: nonpolar/oily (glycine G, alanine A, valine V, leucine L, isoleucine I, methionine M, proline P, phenylalanine F, tryptophan W), polar but uncharged (serine S, threonine T, cysteine C, asparagine N, glutamine Q, tyrosine Y), acidic, negative at body pH (aspartate D, glutamate E), basic (lysine K, arginine R, histidine H; His is mostly neutral at pH 7.4).

Everyday example: Gloves. A left glove and a right glove have the same parts but cannot be swapped. A factory line that only makes left gloves is like your ribosomes, which only use L-amino acids. A plain mitten with no thumb (glycine) fits either hand.

Worked example (step by step): Is L-alanine R or S?

  1. List the four groups on the α-carbon: –NH₂, –COOH, –CH₃, –H.
  2. Rank by atomic number of the first atom: N (7) beats C (6), so –NH₂ is #1. Between the two carbons, –COOH has (O, O, O) attached and –CH₃ has (H, H, H), so –COOH is #2 and –CH₃ is #3. –H is #4.
  3. Point H away from you and trace 1 → 2 → 3. For L-alanine this runs counterclockwise, so it is S.

MCAT trap: "L means S." They are separate systems. L-cysteine is R.

Practice in the 5,904-question Qbank (80% passage): (which amino acid is achiral), (L configuration in human proteins).

Concept 2: Charge, pKa and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

In plain English: Some parts of an amino acid can hold an extra H⁺ (and become more positive) or give it away (and become more negative). Whether they hold it depends on how acidic the surroundings are. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation lets you calculate exactly how many hold it.

Analogy: Each chargeable group is a coat hook holding one coat (H⁺). The pKa says how tightly the hook grips. In a room crowded with coats (low pH, lots of H⁺), hooks stay full. In an empty room (high pH), coats drift away.

Official definition: The ratio of deprotonated to protonated forms of an acidic group depends on the difference between the solution pH and the group's pKa, as described by the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Compare pH to pKa. pH below pKa → group mostly holds its H⁺ (protonated). pH above pKa → mostly lost it (deprotonated). pH equal to pKa → exactly 50/50.
  • At body pH (7.4) the carboxyl end (pKa ≈ 2) has lost its H⁺ (COO⁻, negative) and the amino end (pKa ≈ 9–10) still holds it (NH₃⁺, positive). A free amino acid in blood is therefore a zwitterion.
  • Every 1 unit of difference = 10 times the ratio. 1 unit apart is 10 : 1, 2 units is 100 : 1, 3 units is 1,000 : 1.
pH = pKa + log ( [A⁻] / [HA] )

In plain words: the acidity of the solution equals the group's "grip strength" plus a correction for how many molecules have let go of their H⁺ versus how many are still holding it.

When to use it: any time a question gives you a pH and a pKa and asks what fraction is charged, protonated or deprotonated, or asks for the pH of a buffer (a mix of a weak acid and its partner base). Classic MCAT uses: amino acid charge at a given pH, blood buffer (bicarbonate), drug absorption. When it does not apply: strong acids or bases (like HCl or NaOH), which let go of H⁺ completely; and it gets unreliable when the acid or base is extremely dilute or the ratio is more extreme than about 1,000 : 1.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
pHHow acidic the solution is (−log of the H⁺ concentration)noneLow number = crowded with H⁺
pKaThe pH at which this group is half protonated, half deprotonatednoneGrip strength: low pKa = weak grip, lets H⁺ go easily
[A⁻]Concentration of the form that has given up H⁺ (the base form)M (moles per liter)Empty hooks
[HA]Concentration of the form still holding H⁺ (the acid form)MFull hooks
logBase-10 logarithm: log(10) = 1, log(100) = 2, log(1) = 0noneCounts "how many times 10"

Everyday example: The earthquake (Richter) scale: a magnitude 6 is 10 times stronger than a 5, and 100 times stronger than a 4. pH works the same way. If the pH is 2 units above the pKa, then for every 1 molecule still holding its H⁺ there are 100 that have let go, like 100 empty coat hooks for every 1 full one.

MCAT worked example (step by step, no calculator): In a solution at pH 7.0, what fraction of histidine side chains (pKa 6.0) carry H⁺ (and are positive)?

Formula → variables → substitution → answer:

pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])
  1. Variables: pH = 7.0, pKa = 6.0, and we want [A⁻]/[HA].
  2. Substitute: 7.0 = 6.0 + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 7.0 − 6.0 = 1.
  3. Undo the log: log(10) = 1, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10¹ = 10. That is 10 without H⁺ for every 1 with H⁺.
  4. Fraction with H⁺ = 1/(10 + 1) = 1/11 ≈ 9%. About 91% have let go of H⁺.

Kid-level trick: the pH is exactly 1 above the pKa, and 1 unit means “10 times”: 10 empty hooks for every 1 full hook. Total hooks = 11, so full hooks = 1 out of 11.

Body-pH note: at blood pH 7.4 (1.4 above the pKa) histidine is even more deprotonated, so it is mostly neutral. Exactly one pH unit from the pKa is the case you can do by hand.

MCAT trap: Flipping the ratio. It is base over acid ([A⁻]/[HA]). Putting [HA] on top gives the opposite answer.

pI = (pKa₁ + pKa₂) / 2

In plain words: the pH at which a molecule has zero net charge is the average of the two pKa values on either side of its neutral form.

When to use it: questions asking for the pI of an amino acid or peptide, or which way a protein moves in an electric field (electrophoresis): at a pH below its pI a protein is positive and moves toward the negative electrode; above its pI it is negative. When it does not apply: you must pick the right two pKa values. Do not average all three for amino acids with a charged side chain.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
pIIsoelectric point: pH where net charge = 0noneThe balance point where the molecule stops moving in an electric field
pKa₁, pKa₂The two pKa values just below and just above the net-zero formnoneNeutral side chain: the α-COOH and α-NH₃⁺ values. Acidic (aspartate D, glutamate E): the two lowest. Basic (lysine K, arginine R, histidine H): the two highest

Everyday example: Two towns sit at mile 2 and mile 10 on a highway. The fair meeting point is halfway, mile 6. The pI is the halfway point between the two pKa "towns" that surround the neutral form.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. Glycine has pKa values 2.34 (α-COOH) and 9.60 (α-NH₃⁺). Its side chain (H) has no charge, so use both: pI = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97.
  2. Aspartate has pKa values 1.9, 3.7 (side chain) and 9.6. It is acidic, so the neutral form sits between the two lowest: pI = (1.9 + 3.7)/2 = 2.8.

MCAT trap: Averaging all three pKa values for an acidic or basic amino acid. Only the two pKa values that bracket the net-zero form count.

Practice in the 5,904-question Qbank (80% passage): (pI of glycine), (pI of glutamate), (pI of arginine), (net charge of lysine at pH 7), (net charge of a tripeptide).

Concept 3: Peptide bonds and the four levels of protein structure

In plain English: Amino acids snap together into a chain through peptide bonds. The chain then folds in stages: first into local coils and sheets, then into a full 3D shape, and sometimes several chains join together. Folding happens on its own because it lowers free energy, mostly by freeing water molecules.

Analogy: A protein is a sentence folded into a paper sculpture. The order of the letters (primary structure) is fixed in ink (strong covalent bonds). Pleats and spirals in the paper (secondary), the shape of the whole sculpture (tertiary), and several sculptures glued together (quaternary) are held by weaker, reversible forces, so heat or chemicals can unfold them without erasing the letters.

Official definition: Primary structure is the covalent amino acid sequence; secondary is local backbone hydrogen bonding (α-helix, β-sheet); tertiary is the 3D fold set by side-chain interactions; quaternary is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits.

Core idea (3 points):

  • The peptide bond forms by condensation (one water released). Electrons are shared across the C–N bond (resonance), giving it partial double-bond character, so it is flat, rigid and usually trans (the side groups sit on opposite sides). Breaking it with water (hydrolysis) is favorable but extremely slow without an enzyme.
  • Secondary structure uses H-bonds between backbone N–H and C=O groups (α-helix, β-sheet). Proline breaks helices (it has no N–H and its ring is rigid); glycine adds flexibility (common in turns).
  • Tertiary structure is held by the hydrophobic effect (main driver: oily side chains hide inside), salt bridges (+ and − side chains attracting), H-bonds and disulfide bonds (covalent S–S links between two cysteines, common in proteins sent outside the cell). Denaturation (heat, extreme pH, urea, detergent) destroys 2°–4° structure but leaves the 1° sequence intact.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS

In plain words: whether a process happens on its own (ΔG) depends on the heat it gives off or absorbs (ΔH) minus the temperature times the change in disorder (TΔS).

When to use it: any "is this spontaneous?" or "at what temperature does it become spontaneous?" question: protein folding, dissolving, melting, binding, ATP hydrolysis. Also to explain the hydrophobic effect. When it does not apply: it tells you whether a process can happen, not how fast. A negative ΔG reaction can still take years (peptide hydrolysis without an enzyme). T must be in kelvin.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
ΔGChange in Gibbs free energy (the "Δ" means "change in")kJ/molNegative = happens on its own (spontaneous); positive = needs an energy input
ΔHEnthalpy change: heat released (−) or absorbed (+)kJ/molNegative = gives off heat, which helps
TAbsolute temperatureK (kelvin = °C + 273)The "volume knob" on how much disorder matters
ΔSEntropy change: how much more spread out or disordered things getkJ/(mol·K) (tables often list J, so divide by 1,000)Positive = more freedom and mess, which helps

Everyday example: Ice melting. Melting absorbs heat (ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol, unfavorable) but makes the water molecules freer (ΔS = +0.0220 kJ/(mol·K), favorable). On a warm 25 °C day (298 K): ΔG = 6.01 − 298 × 0.0220 = −0.55 kJ/mol, so ice melts on its own. In a −10 °C freezer (263 K): ΔG = 6.01 − 263 × 0.0220 = +0.22 kJ/mol, so it stays frozen. At 0 °C (273 K) ΔG ≈ 0: ice and water are balanced. Temperature decides which term wins.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Burying an oily side chain inside a protein releases water molecules that were held in a tight cage around it. Suppose ΔH = +10 kJ/mol and ΔS = +50 J/(mol·K) at body temperature, 310 K.

  1. Convert ΔS to kJ: 50 J = 0.050 kJ, so ΔS = 0.050 kJ/(mol·K).
  2. TΔS = 310 × 0.050 = 15.5 kJ/mol.
  3. ΔG = 10 − 15.5 = −5.5 kJ/mol. Folding is favorable because the water's freedom goes up, even though heat is absorbed.

MCAT trap: Forgetting to convert ΔS from J to kJ. Using 50 instead of 0.050 gives ΔG = −15,490 kJ/mol, an impossible number.

Practice in the 5,904-question Qbank (80% passage): (forming a peptide bond), (peptide bond geometry), (why proteins survive in water), (tertiary structure), (disulfides in secreted proteins), (how urea denatures).

Concept 4: How enzymes speed up reactions

In plain English: Enzymes make reactions faster by lowering the energy hill the reaction has to climb. They do not change where the reaction ends up or how much energy it releases.

Analogy: An enzyme is a tunnel through a mountain. The towns on either side (start and finish) stay at the same height (same ΔG), but travelers no longer have to climb over the peak (lower activation energy), so many more cross per hour.

Official definition: Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower the activation energy (Ea) by stabilizing the transition state (the unstable halfway point of the reaction); they do not change ΔG, the equilibrium constant or the equilibrium position.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Same destination, faster trip. Enzymes speed the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so equilibrium (the point where both directions balance) is reached sooner but sits in the same place.
  • How they do it: grip the transition state tightly, hold reacting groups in the right position, donate or accept H⁺ (acid–base catalysis), briefly bond to the substrate (covalent catalysis), or use metal ions.
  • Helpers: cofactors are inorganic helpers (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺); coenzymes are organic helpers, often made from vitamins (NAD⁺ from niacin). An enzyme without its helper is an apoenzyme; with it, a holoenzyme.

Everyday example: A match and a pile of wood. Wood burning releases lots of energy (very negative ΔG), yet a log sits in the air for years without catching fire because the activation energy is high. A match (like an enzyme) gets it over the hill. The match does not change how much heat the fire gives off.

Worked example (step by step): A reaction has ΔG°′ = −20 kJ/mol. An enzyme lowers Ea from 80 to 50 kJ/mol.

  1. ΔG°′ depends only on start and end, so it stays −20 kJ/mol.
  2. The equilibrium constant K′eq depends only on ΔG°′, so it is unchanged.
  3. Only the rate changes: it goes up (a lot, because rate depends exponentially on Ea).

MCAT trap: "The enzyme made the reaction more favorable." It made it faster, not more favorable.

Practice in the 5,904-question Qbank (80% passage): (fast vs. favorable for peptide hydrolysis).

Concept 5: Michaelis–Menten kinetics (how fast an enzyme works)

In plain English: The more substrate you give an enzyme, the faster it works, but only up to a limit. Once every enzyme is busy, adding more substrate does not help. Two numbers describe an enzyme: its top speed (Vmax) and how much substrate it needs to reach half of that speed (Km).

Analogy: A supermarket with a fixed number of cashiers (enzymes) and shoppers (substrate) arriving. With few shoppers, cashiers stand idle and checkouts per minute rise with every extra shopper. With a crowd, every cashier is busy and checkouts max out (Vmax). Km is the crowd size at which the cashiers are busy half the time.

Official definition: For a single-substrate enzyme at steady state, the initial velocity rises hyperbolically with substrate concentration and approaches Vmax; Km is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Two zones: at low [S] (much less than Km), speed rises almost in a straight line with [S] (first order). At high [S] (much more than Km), speed is stuck near Vmax (zero order: more S changes nothing).
  • Km measures "affinity": a lower Km means the enzyme reaches half speed with less substrate, so it grabs substrate more readily.
  • Vmax depends on how much enzyme you have. kcat (turnover number) is the speed of one enzyme molecule and does not depend on amount.
v = Vmax · [S] / (Km + [S])

In plain words: the enzyme's speed equals its top speed times the fraction of time it is busy, and that fraction is [S]/(Km + [S]).

When to use it: questions giving Km, Vmax and [S] and asking for the speed, or asking what [S] gives a certain fraction of Vmax. Shortcuts: [S] = Km gives ½Vmax; [S] = 3Km gives ¾Vmax; [S] = 9Km gives 90% of Vmax. When it does not apply: cooperative (allosteric) enzymes with S-shaped curves, such as hemoglobin-like binding (use the Hill equation, Concept 7). It describes the initial speed, before product builds up.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
v (v₀)Initial reaction speed (velocity)M/s, μM/s or μmol/minCheckouts per minute right now
VmaxTop speed when every enzyme is busy (saturated)same as vAll cashiers working nonstop
[S]Substrate concentrationM, mM or μMNumber of shoppers in the store
KmMichaelis constant: the [S] at which v = ½Vmaxsame units as [S]Small Km = enzyme gets busy even with few shoppers

Everyday example: A store's 4 cashiers can check out at most 4 shoppers per minute (Vmax = 4/min). They are busy half the time when 10 shoppers are in the store (Km = 10). With 30 shoppers: v = 4 × 30/(10 + 30) = 4 × 0.75 = 3 shoppers per minute. Tripling the crowd from 10 to 30 only raised speed from 2 to 3, because the cashiers were already filling up.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Km = 2 mM, Vmax = 100 μmol/min, [S] = 6 mM.

  1. Check units: [S] and Km are both in mM. Good.
  2. Fraction busy = 6/(2 + 6) = 0.75.
  3. v = 100 × 0.75 = 75 μmol/min. Check with the shortcut: [S] = 3Km gives ¾Vmax. ✓

MCAT trap: Mixing units. [S] and Km must be in the same unit (both mM or both μM) before you divide.

1/v = (Km / Vmax) · (1/[S]) + 1/Vmax

In plain words: if you flip both the speed and the substrate amount upside down (take 1 over each), the curved Michaelis–Menten graph becomes a straight line, and Km and Vmax can be read straight off where the line crosses the axes. This is the Lineweaver–Burk (double reciprocal) plot.

When to use it: questions showing a Lineweaver–Burk graph and asking for Km or Vmax, or asking which type of inhibitor a set of lines shows (Concept 6). When it does not apply: cooperative enzymes do not give a straight line.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
1/vy-axis: time per unit of products/MBigger = slower enzyme
1/[S]x-axis1/MBigger = less substrate
Km/VmaxSlope of the linesSteeper = worse at low [S]
1/VmaxWhere the line crosses the y-axiss/MHigher crossing = lower top speed
−1/KmWhere the line crosses the x-axis (always negative)1/MCloser to zero = larger Km

Everyday example: Instead of "shoppers checked out per minute", count "minutes per shopper". The store above has a top speed of 4 per minute, which flips to 0.25 minutes per shopper, the fastest possible. That is the y-intercept (1/Vmax). Flipping turns "speed" into "time per item", and time per item falls in a straight line as the store gets busier.

MCAT worked example (step by step): A Lineweaver–Burk line crosses the x-axis at −0.5 mM⁻¹ and the y-axis at 0.02 min/μmol.

  1. x-intercept = −1/Km = −0.5, so Km = 1/0.5 = 2 mM.
  2. y-intercept = 1/Vmax = 0.02, so Vmax = 1/0.02 = 50 μmol/min.

MCAT trap: Reading the x-intercept as +1/Km. It is −1/Km, on the negative side.

kcat = Vmax / [E]totalefficiency = kcat / Km

In plain words: kcat is how many substrate molecules one enzyme can process per second at top speed. Dividing by Km gives catalytic efficiency, which rewards an enzyme for being both fast and good at grabbing substrate.

When to use it: questions giving Vmax and enzyme concentration and asking for turnover, or asking which of two enzymes is "more efficient" or "better at low substrate". When it does not apply: kcat/Km compares enzymes at low [S]; at saturating [S], kcat alone decides speed.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
kcatTurnover number: substrate molecules converted per active site per seconds⁻¹ (per second)Speed of one worker
[E]totalTotal enzyme (active site) concentrationMHow many workers you hired
kcat/KmCatalytic efficiency (specificity constant)M⁻¹s⁻¹Best single score for comparing enzymes; the physical upper limit is about 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ (set by how fast molecules bump into each other)

Everyday example: A bakery with 10 ovens can make at most 600 loaves per hour. Each oven's turnover is 600/10 = 60 loaves per hour. Hiring more ovens raises the bakery's maximum (Vmax) but not each oven's speed (kcat).

MCAT worked example (step by step): Vmax = 1 × 10⁻⁵ M/s and [E]total = 5 × 10⁻⁹ M.

  1. kcat = (1 × 10⁻⁵)/(5 × 10⁻⁹) = 2,000 s⁻¹ (each enzyme handles 2,000 molecules per second).
  2. If Km = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M: kcat/Km = 2,000/(1 × 10⁻⁴) = 2 × 10⁷ M⁻¹s⁻¹, close to the diffusion limit, so this enzyme is very efficient.

MCAT trap: Comparing enzymes by Km alone. The enzyme with the highest kcat/Km is the most efficient, even if its Km is not the lowest.

Practice in the 5,904-question Qbank (80% passage): (defining Km), (v at [S] = 6 mM), (v at [S] = Km/3), (order at high [S]), (kcat), (catalytic efficiency).

Concept 6: Enzyme inhibition

In plain English: Inhibitors slow enzymes. Some block the active site (competitive), so piling on more substrate wins. Others jam the enzyme somewhere else (noncompetitive), so more substrate does not help. Which kind it is changes Km, Vmax, or both.

Analogy: Back at the supermarket: a competitive inhibitor is a person who stands in the checkout line only to ask for directions. Send in enough real shoppers and they crowd those people out. A noncompetitive inhibitor is a broken card reader: the lane is out of action no matter how many shoppers come. An uncompetitive inhibitor only jams a register that already has a shopper at it.

Official definition: Competitive inhibitors bind the free enzyme's active site (raise apparent Km, Vmax unchanged); pure noncompetitive inhibitors bind E and ES equally at another site (lower Vmax, Km unchanged); uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the enzyme–substrate complex ES (lower both by the same factor); mixed inhibitors bind E and ES unequally.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Competitive inhibition can be beaten by adding lots of substrate; noncompetitive cannot.
  • "Apparent" Km is the Km you measure with inhibitor present. It changes because some enzyme is tied up; the enzyme's true grip on substrate is not changed.
  • Lineweaver–Burk patterns: competitive lines cross on the y-axis (same Vmax); noncompetitive lines cross on the x-axis (same Km); uncompetitive lines are parallel.
Km,app = Km · (1 + [I]/Ki)(competitive)

In plain words: a competitive inhibitor makes it look as if the enzyme needs more substrate to reach half speed, by a factor of (1 + inhibitor amount ÷ inhibitor strength).

When to use it: questions about a competitive inhibitor (binds the active site, "resembles the substrate", "overcome by excess substrate") asking for the new Km or the new speed. Vmax stays the same. When it does not apply: noncompetitive or uncompetitive inhibitors (use the next formula or the summary table in Section B).

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
Km,appKm measured with inhibitor presentMLooks like weaker grip
KmKm without inhibitorMNormal value

Everyday example: The cashiers above were busy half the time with 10 real shoppers (Km = 10). Direction-askers arrive in a number equal to Ki. Now you need 20 real shoppers to keep cashiers half busy (10 × (1 + 1)). But if 1,000 shoppers flood in, the cashiers still reach their top speed of 4 per minute, so Vmax is unchanged.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Km = 4 μM, Vmax = 80 μM/s, [I] = Ki, [S] = 4 μM.

  1. Factor = 1 + [I]/Ki = 1 + 1 = 2. Km,app = 4 × 2 = 8 μM.
  2. v = 80 × 4/(8 + 4) = 26.7 μM/s.
  3. Compare: without inhibitor, v = 80 × 4/(4 + 4) = 40 μM/s.

MCAT trap: Using [I]/Ki alone instead of 1 + [I]/Ki. At [I] = Ki that would predict no change, which is wrong.

Vmax,app = Vmax / (1 + [I]/Ki)(pure noncompetitive)

In plain words: a noncompetitive inhibitor takes enzymes out of action, so the top speed drops by the same factor (1 + [I]/Ki), while Km stays the same.

When to use it: questions about an inhibitor that binds away from the active site (allosteric site) and "cannot be overcome by adding substrate", asking for the new Vmax or speed. When it does not apply: competitive inhibitors (Vmax does not change) or mixed inhibitors (Km changes too).

Everyday example: A store has 3 registers. Card readers fail so that only 1 in 3 works (factor 3, as when [I] = 2Ki). The top speed drops from 3 to 1 shopper per minute, and no number of extra shoppers can fix a broken register.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Vmax = 120 μM/s, [I] = 2Ki.

  1. Factor = 1 + 2 = 3. Vmax,app = 120/3 = 40 μM/s.
  2. Km is unchanged, so at [S] = Km the speed is half of the new Vmax: 20 μM/s.

MCAT trap: Saying noncompetitive inhibitors "bind the active site". They bind elsewhere, which is why adding substrate cannot outcompete them.

Concept 7: Cooperativity and allosteric regulation

In plain English: Some proteins have several binding sites that "talk" to each other. Once one site grabs a molecule, the others grab more easily. This makes the binding curve S-shaped instead of a smooth curve, so a small change in the amount of molecule causes a big change in how full the protein is.

Analogy: A group of friends at a party. Nobody wants to dance first, but once one person starts, the others join in more easily. Binding at one site makes binding at the next site easier.

Official definition: In cooperative binding, ligand binding at one subunit raises the affinity of other subunits, producing a sigmoidal (S-shaped) binding or velocity curve; the Hill coefficient measures the degree of cooperativity.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Hill coefficient n: n > 1 = positive cooperativity (hemoglobin, n ≈ 2.8); n = 1 = no cooperativity (myoglobin, a single-site protein); n < 1 = negative cooperativity.
  • Allosteric regulators bind somewhere other than the active site. Activators shift the curve left (active at lower [S]); inhibitors shift it right.
  • Why it matters: an S-shaped curve acts like a switch. Hemoglobin loads O₂ fully in the lungs and dumps a lot in the tissues, where O₂ is only somewhat lower.
θ = [L]ⁿ / (K₀.₅ⁿ + [L]ⁿ)

In plain words: the fraction of binding sites that are filled depends on how much ligand is around compared with the half-full level, raised to the power n, which sets how switch-like the response is.

When to use it: questions on hemoglobin O₂ binding, allosteric enzymes with S-shaped curves, or "what does a Hill coefficient of 2.8 or 1 mean". When it does not apply: the Hill coefficient describes steepness; it is not a count of binding sites. For simple one-site enzymes use Michaelis–Menten (it is the special case n = 1).

[L]Ligand concentration (or partial pressure, such as PO₂ for oxygen)M or mmHgHow much ligand is around
K₀.₅[L] at which half the sites are filledsame as [L]Like Km, but for binding

Everyday example: A stadium wave. With n = 1, people stand up one at a time on their own schedule. With n = 3, once a few stand, everyone near them jumps up too. At twice the "halfway" level, the n = 1 crowd is 67% standing but the n = 3 crowd is 89% standing.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Compare n = 1 and n = 3 at [L] = 2 × K₀.₅.

  1. n = 1: θ = 2/(1 + 2) = 0.67.
  2. n = 3: θ = 2³/(1 + 2³) = 8/9 = 0.89.
  3. Conclusion: cooperativity makes the protein fill much faster above K₀.₅ (and empty faster below it).

MCAT trap: Thinking n equals the number of binding sites. Hemoglobin has 4 sites but n ≈ 2.8.

C) 3 MCAT-STYLE PRACTICE QUESTIONS

Q1. A researcher measures an enzyme with Km = 4 μM and Vmax = 80 μM/s. A competitive inhibitor is added at [I] = 3Ki. What is the initial velocity at [S] = 4 μM?

  • A) 10 μM/s
  • B) 16 μM/s
  • C) 20 μM/s
  • D) 40 μM/s

Answer: B. Km,app = 4(1 + 3) = 16 μM. v = 80 × 4/(16 + 4) = 16 μM/s.

  • A is wrong: 10 μM/s treats the inhibitor as noncompetitive (Vmax/(1 + 3) = 20 μM/s, then halved because [S] = Km).
  • B is correct: the apparent Km is quadrupled while Vmax is unchanged.
  • C is wrong: 20 μM/s comes from multiplying Km by 3 instead of by (1 + 3), giving Km,app = 12 μM.
  • D is wrong: 40 μM/s is ½Vmax, the velocity at [S] = Km with no inhibitor present.

Q2. A protein unfolds in 8 M urea and refolds correctly when the urea is dialyzed away. Which conclusion is best supported?

  • A) Urea hydrolyzed the peptide bonds, which re-formed after dialysis.
  • B) The primary sequence contains the information needed to reach the native fold.
  • C) The protein's disulfide bonds were reduced by urea.
  • D) The native state has higher free energy than the unfolded state.

Answer: B. This is the logic of Anfinsen's experiment: the sequence alone directs folding.

  • A is wrong: urea disrupts noncovalent interactions; it does not hydrolyze peptide bonds.
  • B is correct: refolding without any other template shows sequence determines structure.
  • C is wrong: urea is not a reducing agent; β-mercaptoethanol is what reduces disulfides in that classic experiment.
  • D is wrong: spontaneous refolding means the native state is lower in free energy under physiological conditions.

Q3. At pH 7.4, which residue in a polypeptide would most likely form a salt bridge with a lysine side chain?

  • A) Glutamine
  • B) Aspartate
  • C) Histidine
  • D) Serine

Answer: B. Lysine is +1 at pH 7.4, so it pairs with a negatively charged side chain.

  • A is wrong: glutamine is an amide and stays uncharged.
  • B is correct: the aspartate side chain (pKa ≈ 3.9) is −1 at pH 7.4.
  • C is wrong: histidine (pKa ≈ 6) is mostly neutral at pH 7.4 and would be positive when charged, so it would repel lysine.
  • D is wrong: serine's hydroxyl is polar but uncharged; it can H-bond but cannot form a salt bridge.
